strengths: Clear practical motivation: Addresses synthetic survival data generation, an important but understudied problem in medical ML with real clinical applications
Solid end-to-end framework: Avoids multi-stage error propagation of SurvivalGAN by jointly optimizing covariate fidelity and survival structure

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple metrics (covariate fidelity, downstream performance, survival-specific), three datasets with varying censoring rates, 10 seeds with proper statistical reporting
Consistent improvements: Shows clear gains over SurvivalGAN (main baseline) across most metrics; particularly strong on high-censoring datasets
Robust to small-sample settings: Demonstrates benefits in downsampled scenarios, important for medical applications
Good engineering execution: Appropriate handling of mixed-type variables, practical design choices (adaptive loss weighting), stable training (Figure 9)
Well-presented: Clear writing, informative architecture diagrams, extensive supplementary materials with ablations
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: Diffusion process largely copied from TabDiff without modification; survival loss is primary novelty but a relatively straightforward Cox PH extension

Insufficient theoretical justification: Why does optimizing Cox partial likelihood during diffusion training produce better synthetic survival data? Cox optimizes rank correlation, not curve calibration
Mismatch between loss and evaluation: Table 7 shows SURVDIFF has better C-index but worse/comparable Kaplan-Meier MSE than TabDiff, suggesting the loss may optimize the wrong objective for this task

Critical ablations missing: No ablation comparing standard Cox loss (w=1) vs. sparsity-weighted version; no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters α and τ in Eq. 11; limited analysis of λ_surv contribution
Strong unaddressed assumption: Method assumes independent censoring (MAR), which is often violated in practice (treatment withdrawal, loss-to-follow-up correlations) but receives no discussion

Narrow experimental scope: All three datasets are medical (two breast cancer); no evaluation on non-medical survival data; relatively small sample sizes (600-2000); no domain expert validation of synthetic data clinical validity
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices: α_surv=0.3, warm-up epochs 1500/4000 lack justification; τ in Eq. 11 has no default specified; λ_cont, λ_disc selection not discussed
Reproducibility concerns: No code availability statement; computational cost only briefly mentioned; some implementation details relegated to supplement; several modeling choices unexplained

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: Fills genuine gap as first end-to-end diffusion model for survival data generation

Sound technical approach with proper handling of mixed-type variables (discrete event indicator via masking, continuous event times via Gaussian diffusion) and survival-tailored loss incorporating Cox partial likelihood with sparsity-aware weighting
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple metrics (covariate fidelity, downstream performance, survival metrics) with proper statistical reporting (10 seeds, standard deviations)
Strong and clinically relevant performance on high-censoring datasets (AIDS 91.7%, GBSG2 56.4%) and demonstrated robustness in small-sample regimes (Appendix E)
End-to-end learning avoids error propagation issues of prior multi-step approaches like SurvivalGAN
Reproducibility: Complete implementation details, comprehensive hyperparameters, and stable training dynamics demonstrated
Clear presentation with good clinical contextualization of why synthetic survival data is important for medical research
weaknesses: Mixed experimental results on largest dataset (METABRIC): C-Index essentially tied with TabDiff, Brier score worse than TabDiff, and critically RMST gap 5.6× worse than TabDiff (0.0268 vs 0.0048)—concerning underperformance on survival-specific metric that deserves more discussion

Limited architectural novelty: Primarily combines existing components (TabDiff's mixed-type handling + masked diffusion) with the main contribution being loss function design rather than novel model architecture

Critical missing ablation studies: No ablations on loss components (diffusion vs survival loss contribution), sparsity-aware weighting scheme, or sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (α, τ, α_surv)

Insufficient analysis of when and why method succeeds/fails: Performance varies substantially across datasets but underlying causes (censoring rates, data characteristics) are suggested but not rigorously investigated

Inadequate treatment of ethical and privacy concerns: For medical applications, lacks discussion of re-identification risks, privacy guarantees, fairness/bias preservation, and privacy-utility tradeoffs despite claiming to enable data sharing
Limited evaluation scope: Only 3 cancer-related datasets with modest sizes (686-1903 patients); generalization to other medical domains and larger datasets unclear
Theoretical gaps: Why discriminative loss (Cox regression) improves generative model training not explained; formal justification for sparsity-aware weighting scheme lacking

Incomplete technical details: Post-hoc administrative censoring mentioned but not explained; scalability to high-dimensional or high-cardinality categorical data unclear; computational cost comparison with baselines absent
Hyperparameter robustness: While λ_surv uses adaptive scaling, sensitivity to α, τ, and α_surv across datasets unexplored, limiting practical applicability
Inconsistent claims: Paper states 'consistently outperforms' but METABRIC results show on-par or worse performance on multiple key metrics
